difficultyRationale: Tests a foundational structural trade-off between contiguous and pointer-based storage, without requiring any implementation detail.
prompt: A backend job scheduler repeatedly inserts new jobs at the front of a very large in-memory job list. Comparing a singly linked list to a dynamic array (contiguous storage) for this exact workload, what is the main structural reason the linked list performs the insertion faster?
explanation: Inserting at the front of a linked list only requires allocating a new node and updating one pointer, which is O(1) regardless of list size. A dynamic array stores elements contiguously, so inserting at the front requires shifting every existing element one position to the right, which is O(n).

options.text: The linked list's front insertion is O(1) because it only creates a new node and relinks a pointer, with no need to move any existing elements.
options.explanation: Correct: because nodes are connected by pointers rather than stored in contiguous slots, adding a new head node never requires relocating the other elements.

options.text: The linked list's front insertion is O(1) because linked lists always keep a block of pre-allocated free slots at the beginning for future insertions.
options.explanation: This describes a mechanism linked lists don't use. Linked lists don't pre-reserve empty slots; each node is allocated individually when needed, which is exactly why no shifting is required.

options.text: The linked list's front insertion is O(log n) because the list keeps itself balanced like a search tree to speed up traversal.
options.explanation: A plain singly linked list has no balancing concept at all — it is not a tree and has no notion of height or balance factor. Front insertion is O(1), not O(log n).

options.text: Both structures require O(n) time for front insertion, so there is no structural advantage either way.
options.explanation: This denies a real difference: the dynamic array does need O(n) to shift existing elements on front insertion, but the linked list does not, since it has no contiguous layout to preserve.
